analysis.one_liner: Makes permanent the court-order requirement protecting servicemembers from foreclosure after deployment.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the final weeks of the 113th Congress with no cosponsors, it was referred to a House Veterans' Affairs subcommittee and died there without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Under a 2012 law, a service member who owned a home before entering military service is protected from foreclosure, seizure, or eviction for one year after service ends — a court must approve any such action, or the service member must sign away the protection. That one-year shield was scheduled to shrink back to nine months starting January 1, 2015. This bill would have repealed the provision reverting to the shorter period, keeping the stronger, court-supervised protection in place permanently. It was referred to the House Veterans' Affairs Committee and its Subcommittee on Economic Opportunity, and no further action was taken before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Service members and their families, who would keep protection from having their homes sold or seized without a judge's sign-off for a full year after they leave active duty, rather than seeing that window shrink back to nine months.

how_it_helps.text: Per the CRS summary, the bill repeals the provision that would bring back the shorter nine-month protection period, keeping in place the one-year foreclosure and eviction shield enacted in the 2012 Camp Lejeune Act.

For a service member returning to civilian life, this means a creditor generally must go to court to foreclose on or seize property the member owned before military service, and a sale or foreclosure without such a court order or a signed waiver is invalid during the protection period.

analysis.who_pays: Mortgage lenders and loan servicers, who would face a longer period before they can foreclose on a former service member's home without going to court.

drawbacks.text: The bill's title and text speak of making nine-month protections permanent, while the CRS summary describes the bill as repealing the scheduled revival of the old nine-month period and thereby preserving the 2012 law's one-year protection — a mismatch in how the bill's effect is described that an honest observer would flag.

Extending foreclosure protections imposes some cost on mortgage lenders, who would face longer delays before completing a foreclosure and could face higher losses on loans to borrowers who leave service, costs that could in principle be passed to future borrowers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — preventing mortgage lenders from foreclosing on servicemembers' homes during a window after deployment without court oversight — is significant for affected families and costs lenders little beyond a delay and a court step they already can obtain. The bill's text is short and targeted, and its main weakness is political rather than substantive: it arrived in the final weeks of a Congress with no cosponsors and no committee action, so it never had a realistic path to passage. An honest supporter would also acknowledge the ambiguity between the bill's title (which speaks of nine-month protections) and the CRS reading (preserving the one-year period).

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to a House Veterans' Affairs subcommittee in late November 2014, with no cosponsors and only weeks left in the session, and nothing further ever happened to it.

narrative.text: Rep. Alan Grayson introduced the bill on November 18, 2014, less than seven weeks before the 113th Congress ended.
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor.

The House referred it to the Veterans' Affairs Committee on November 18, 2014, and a week later to its Subcommittee on Economic Opportunity; no further action was taken before the Congress ended on January 3, 2015.
The bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage lenders and servicers, who keep the status quo rather than face a permanent requirement to obtain a court order or a signed waiver before foreclosing on returning servicemembers' property. No one else gains.

for.name: Rep. Alan Grayson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the final weeks of the 113th Congress and referred it to committee.

sides.party_line_note: The bill attracted no cosponsors and no committee or floor action, so no partisan split was ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill would keep a rule requiring lenders to obtain a court order or a signed waiver before foreclosing on a returning servicemember's property, limiting repossession but not eliminating it. Lenders lose some speed and discretion in foreclosures; affected families gain protection from losing their homes without a judge's review.

Second look at the mechanism: the direct effect on the industry is a modest loss — a longer court-supervised window before foreclosure — while the corresponding benefit accrues to individual servicemembers. There is no offsetting gain for lenders.
